articles.fullContent: 当Notable Capital将其超过10亿美元的基金中约10%的美国份额投入Anthropic的E轮融资时，许多有限合伙人都对这笔巨额押注感到困惑。 Claude 的开发商仍落后于其最大竞争对手 OpenAI，而 DeepSeek 仅在几周前发布了其 R1 模型，有超越闭源竞争对手的势头。此外，以 61 美元的价格， 50亿美元，Anthropic的估值是这家主要投资早期阶段的风险投资公司在其25年历史中迄今为止最高的投资估值。 但在Notable（2024年与中国业务分拆前名为GGV资本）的投资者对Anthropic的未来充满信心。 由管理合伙人Hans Tung和Glenn Solomon以及负责人Dan Cahana组成的团队对数据进行了分析，发现开发者越来越倾向于使用Claude而非ChatGPT，Claude的使用率达到了70%，与前一年相比发生了逆转。 该公司的联合创始人Tung在接受TechCrunch采访时表示：“我们只是知道，对于人工智能来说，开发者是核心，因为他们是早期采用者。” 在应对美国复杂的 -中国关系的亲身经历，Notable还深信，“任务关键型”工作始终需要基于美国的闭源模型，Tung表示。 不到两年后，Notable的有限合伙人不再对这笔巨额投资提出质疑。 周三，Anthropic在有史以来规模最大的IPO中筹集了813亿美元，在其股票于次日开始交易之前，其完全摊薄估值达到约1.5万亿美元，账面回报约为15倍。 当然，Notable 并不是唯一一家从 Anthropic 获得巨额账面收益的公司。 即使是很少看到风险投资规模倍数的传统后期投资者，也注定会大获全胜。 新加坡主权财富基金GIC在2024年全年都在研究Anthropic，但直到2025年初，该基金的技术投资主管Chris Emanuel在旧金山的一家意大利餐厅Che Fico与Anthropic首席财务官Krishna Rao会面后，才进行了首次投资。 Rao向Emanuel展示了模型改进如何推动企业采用率的提升，从而激发了Emanuel对该公司的兴趣。 随后，GIC对Anthropic的F轮融资进行了首次投资，该轮融资于2025年9月宣布，估值为1830亿美元。 “当时Claude Code刚刚发布，”Emanuel告诉TechCrunch。 “当时还很早，但即使是那时，我们也能看到它在开发者中非常受欢迎的迹象。 “GIC 对这家人工智能实验室的信心之高，以至于该基金后来与 Coatue 一起领投了 Anthropic 的 G 轮融资，估值为 3800 亿美元，并在 9650 亿美元的 IPO 前融资轮中再次成为联合领投方之一。 据一位熟悉GIC财务状况的人士透露，在三轮融资中，GIC向Anthropic投资了超过45亿美元，累计持股比例相当于该公司IPO后约...

articles.fullContent: OpenAI首席科学家雅库布·帕乔基（Jakub Pachocki）在新发布的博客文章中讨论了人工智能发展的潜在局限性，重点关注一种名为“困惑度”的衡量指标。 在一位曾就职于OpenAI和Anthropic的研究员表示这两家公司“拿我们的生命在冒险”之后，放缓人工智能发展成为一个特别热门的话题。甚至Anthropic的IPO申请文件也指出，该技术可能对社会构成“灾难性或生存性风险”。 ”随后，Anthropic首席执行官Dario Amodei发布了一项“掌控前沿”的计划，该计划似乎得到了OpenAI首席执行官Sam Altman和SpaceX首席执行官Elon Musk的支持。 除其他事项外，Amodei呼吁各公司同意“共同的安全标准，以及对不受监管的人工智能发展速度的限制”。 但是，要对人工智能的发展设定速度限制，就需要就如何衡量速度达成一致。 Pachocki的帖子——被Altman称为“OpenAI一段时间以来发布的最重要内容”——表明困惑度（perplexity，不要与同名公司混淆）可能是这种衡量标准。 在帕乔基的论述中，随着技术的进步，那些侧重于人工智能“下游能力”的基准很快就过时了。 但困惑度——“衡量模型平均预测下一个token的准确性；困惑度越低，预测越准确”——仍然“具有信息性”。Pachochki的帖子中包含一张图表，显示了自GPT-3以来OpenAI模型困惑度的下降情况。5. “GPT-4的困惑度约为0. 91，善于高效地利用“链式思维”推理，这促使我们随后有针对性地激发了这种能力，并创造了现代推理模型。”他写道。 “现在，随着我们已将损失降至0.8以下，我们在网络安全和数学等领域看到了颠覆性能力的出现。 因此，在他看来，困惑度可以为“通用智能的共同基准”提供基础，人工智能公司随后可以利用这一基准来确立“共同的限度”。如果将困惑度作为衡量人工智能进步的标准，那么各公司将承诺不越过某个阈值，“直到我们理解和监测人工智能行为的能力达到某个具体的里程碑。” ”当您通过我们文章中的链接购买时，我们可能会赚取一小笔佣金。 这不会影响我们的编辑独立性。 Anthony Ha是TechCrunch的周末编辑。 此前，他曾担任《Adweek》的科技记者、《VentureBeat》的高级编辑、《Hollister Free Lance》的地方政府记者，以及一家风险投资公司的内容副总裁。 他现居纽约市。 您可以通过发送电子邮件至[email protected]与Anthony联系或核实其联系信息。 一家初创公司在印度起诉苹果，原因是“轻点分享”联系人功能 Jagmeet Singh

articles.fullContent: 从远处看，现代人工智能的构建方式似乎与过去几十年中软件的构建方式相似：使用一套多样化的技术来针对特定的功能。 确实有各种各样的方法，但它们大多不是从零开始设计，而是利用来自一个更简单、更难解释的过程的智能：在一个非常庞大的数据语料库上训练一个压缩器（或等效地（在新窗口中打开） ，预测器）。 1 我认为，跟踪训练更好压缩器的进展速度是理解人工智能发展轨迹的关键。 在本文中，我主张将困惑度（或等效的交叉熵损失）确立为一种指标，用于在模型开发者之间进行比较，并为共同的安全标准提供参考。 作为第一步，我将让OpenAI的预训练进展更加透明。 我们对发布内部困惑度测量结果进行了慎重考虑；这样做会让竞争对手更清楚地了解我们的立场，但与在整个行业建立共同的（在新窗口中打开）安全措施的紧迫性相比，这种顾虑显得微不足道。 我们OpenAI希望此举能成为迈向为未来的步伐控制工作建立共同科学基础的一步。 对人工智能发展的看法，一种简单但本质上具有启发性的观点是：首先，人们构建一台大型计算机，然后使用它在一个大型非结构化数据集上对一个模型（压缩器）进行预训练，接着在不同的语境中应用各种技术——如提示、微调或强化学习——以激发该模型的潜在能力。 算法的进步可能会模糊训练阶段之间的界限，但我们仍然可以将人工智能的创造（我之前称之为“外星人的思维”）与随后有针对性的诱导区分开来，因为人工智能具有难以预测的涌现能力。 多年来，我们衡量这一关键“智能基质”进展的主要方式一直保持着显著的稳定性——我们一直在跟踪模型在留出数据集上的困惑度。 2 , 3困惑度衡量的是模型平均预测下一个token的准确性；困惑度越低，预测越准确。 本文开头展示的图表显示了从 GPT-3 开始，这一指标在我们模型中的演变情况。5. 主要通过这一指标来描述的模型能力范围令人惊叹。 GPT-2 在旧数据集上树立了新的困惑度最高水平 4 ，可以说是有史以来第一个能够持续生成连贯文本段落的模型。 下一个重大飞跃是 GPT-3，它能够在给定任务的几个示例的情况下进行上下文学习。 GPT-3.5 在我们当前的主要评估数据集上的对数困惑度约为 0.99，能够进行流利的对话，并构成了最初的 ChatGPT 的基础。GPT-4 的对数困惑度约为 0.

articles.title: 为什么数据中心成为科技巨头遭遇强烈反弹的焦点
articles.originalTitle: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash
articles.summary: 这条新闻与AI 热点相关，值得关注其对产品路线、开发者生态或产业竞争格局的影响。原题：TechCrunch AI：AI 热点相关动态
articles.fullContent: 在新作《超大规模》（Hyperscale）中，记者巴黎·马克斯（Paris Marx）探究了数据中心和生成式人工智能的影响，带领读者走进数据中心内部，并解释了已有数十年历史的计算基础设施为何近期成为政治地雷。 这本书可谓应运而生，因为对数据中心的强烈反弹似乎是最近 中期选举中出现大规模“蓝潮”的诱因之一。 随着民主党人掌握更多的政府权力，这些争论很可能会继续下去。 在接受TechCrunch采访时，马克思将数据中心的建设描述为“从根本上不可持续”且“完全不符合宜居星球的理念”，同时还指出，在人们对科技行业普遍不满的背景下，这些设施显然成为了众矢之的。 毕竟，如果要在您的社区建造数据中心，“它非常具体，非常实在。 “无论您站在政治光谱的哪一端，都没有关系，”Marx说道。 “您将在生活质量、电费账单、用水方面，以及可能在社区周边的噪音方面（如果数据中心屋顶的空调机组发出很大的噪音）感受到这些影响。 ”他还指出，反对数据中心只是针对“科技行业的实体表现”的更广泛运动中最显眼的一部分，[……]无论是反对Flock摄像头在美国各地铺开，还是反对Meta试图让人们戴上的智能眼镜，甚至是反对Waymo正在推出的自动驾驶汽车。 ”在我们的谈话中（我为了篇幅和清晰度进行了编辑），Marx和我讨论了数据中心对环境的影响、科技公司如何应对社区的抵制，以及数据中心内部的实际情况。 我喜欢您对试图进入“超大规模”数据中心内部，然后最终参观[一个数据中心]的描述。 您能否多谈谈那次经历是什么样的？ 您是如何进入的？ 当您真正进入时，有什么让您感到惊讶？ 进入超大规模数据中心并不是世界上最容易的任务。 我与一些比我更早开始研究数据中心的研究人员进行了交谈，他们告诉我，在生成式人工智能兴起之前，以及在最近数据中心受到广泛关注之前，进入数据中心要容易得多。 我给多家公司发了电子邮件，询问是否可以进去看看，但往往没有收到回复，有时则被拒绝。 最后，在参观了弗吉尼亚州北部、爱尔兰等地的一些数据中心的外部之后，我实际上去了新西兰，进入了一个数据中心内部。 最令我印象深刻的是安全级别。 显然，您会认为这是一处真正实现安全化的基础设施，因为里面的数据需要得到妥善保护。显然，[他们]在数据中心周围设有高大的围栏和各种安防摄像头。 但要进去，我必须提前提交护照。
articles.originalSummary: Journalist Paris Marx unpacks his new book "Hyperscale."

articles.fullContent: 今天，我将与The Verge的高级人工智能记者Hayden Field聊聊Anthropic的IPO，这是我们关于人工智能在现实生活中的系列节目的第三期，也是最后一期。 Claude背后的这家人工智能实验室于上周四在纳斯达克上市。 数字非常庞大，但对于这次谈话来说并不那么重要，只是想说，Anthropic已经成为全球最有价值的公司之一。 真正值得关注的是现在发生的事情——以及Anthropic是否能够继续在关注和投资人工智能安全的同时，也成为一家对股东负责的上市公司。 哦，对了，它还要不断增加收入，以便能够继续支付不断增加的计算费用，未来几年这些费用总计约9000亿美元。 所有这些观点之间都存在着一种引人入胜的张力，因此Hayden和我真的努力剖析我们认为Anthropic在应对公开市场的压力时可能会如何应对。 您将听到我们谈论公司的独特公司治理结构，在黄仁勋的持续风波之后，这一点尤为重要。 我们还将探讨为什么OpenAI似乎乐于让Anthropic先上市，以及为什么Anthropic向大客户推销的全部内容都归结为同样的安全性品牌，而这一品牌现在与其业务中以盈利为导向的部分存在冲突。 在开始之前，请帮我一个忙，在YouTube上订阅Decoder，我们每周一和周四都会发布新一期节目。 好的：The Verge高级人工智能记者Hayden Field将谈论Anthropic的IPO和前沿人工智能的经济学。 我们开始吧。本次访谈内容经过少量编辑，以控制篇幅并提高清晰度。 Hayden Field，欢迎再次来到《解码》。 谢谢。很高兴来到这里。 我很高兴今天能和你聊聊，因为这不是纯粹的肥皂剧式戏剧性混乱。 我知道。这就像一件很平常的事情。 这次不是以人物为中心，也不是肥皂剧。 这关乎冷冰冰、硬邦邦的潜在现金。 [笑]好吧，其中还是有一些个性色彩的，因为我们将大量讨论Anthropic的IPO，其中涉及一群个性鲜明的人物，而且他们构建这家公司以抵御资本主义的贪婪压力的方式，我想说，非常另类。 它反映了一些特立独行的人的信念。 没错，绝对是这样。 再次深入研究S-1表格，看看谁在哪个委员会任职，哪些创始人在这里拥有最大的控制权，以及创始人实际上拥有多少控制权，这真的很有意思，而且比看起来要多。 让我们从头开始。 你和我正在IPO当天交谈。 Anthropic是第一家上市的纯人工智能实验室。 他们的IPO定价为每股83美元，股价一路涨至111美元。 等到人们听到这段话时，谁知道实际价格会是多少，但对于所有投资Anthropic的人来说，这确实是一次胜利的庆功。 一大批律师事务所都把主页改成了“恭喜大家！” 你对此有何看法？ 这只是必然会发生的事情，还是一个迹象，表明人工智能泡沫不会破裂？ 人们应该如何看待这个问题？

articles.rawFullText: Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder . Thanks. Great to be here. I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos. I know. It’s like a normal thing that happened. It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash. [Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people. Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem. Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!” What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it? I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later. But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell. I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good. So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better. Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first? Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now. Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that. Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year. I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs. Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work? They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry. But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today. I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power. But either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts. I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute. I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from big cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs. That is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do. That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens? I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for passing on costs to consumers . Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them. This became a thing across the industry, a big outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way. The other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for. They’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to moat them in and hope for the best. What’s interesting there is that consumers are sensitive to price in one way. I think Anthropic’s big business customers, which is where they’ve been historically focused, are sensitive to price in different ways. If you’re paying Anthropic a lot of money, you might want to be able to switch providers quickly and you might demand data sovereignty and all this stuff that big enterprises are thinking about. Anthropic either has to deliver that, which would kill their moat for their big enterprise customers, or say, “We’re so good, you can’t have that.” I’m not sure that they can say the second one yet. That’s why they’re marketing this safe, trustworthy AI line so deeply, because it’s the only thing they’ve really got going for them here. When you have an enterprise customer, most of the time you do have to give them data sovereignty. You can’t trade on their data. There’s a lot of stuff that Anthropic could be doing to make more money that they can’t do when someone is paying that much. I think that’s really why they’re driving home this point of being the safe, trustworthy alternative because that’s the only thing that’s really going to get people to stick around, particularly if they also drive home the cybersecurity tools in an age when everything’s getting hacked all the time. The other interesting thing is even not with huge enterprises, but with small to medium-sized businesses, I’ve been chatting with a bunch of them and they’ve all been creating their own internal tools to kind of track which tasks they need specifically to use an expensive Anthropic model for and which ones they can port over to maybe an open-source model or a really cheap model. So a lot of companies like law firms — and people in a lot of different industries that have small to medium-sized businesses — are literally creating their own internal benchmarks about, “Okay, let’s save money as much as we can to just only put 10 percent of our tasks toward the expensive Anthropic model, and then this 40 percent can go to an open-source model and this 50 percent can go to a mid-tier, cheaper model.” So that’s what’s really interesting to me. People are trying to figure this out on their own and not even sharing those benchmarks publicly because it’s their own way of budgeting. I actually heard Nadella this week say every company will have its own set of evaluations and they will test the models against them and always use the most efficient one and this will become one of the major things that every company does. The flip side to that is I’ve heard Anthropic executives say, “Well, you will always want the frontier model because your competitor will always be using the frontier model and if you use a cheaper one, you’ll be left behind.” And that has always seemed somewhere between naive and idealistic to me because I think a lot of companies do cheap things knowing that their competitors will also do cheap things. I agree completely. Everyone’s being cheap. Yeah, I think if you can get away with good enough, you’re going to find out exactly where good enough is and you will not assume that your competitor is going to eke out a 5 percent advantage by using a more expensive model. Somewhere on the margin is where all of the costs should be and the market will figure it out. Exactly. It just feels like the basics of the business, maybe on IPO day, the pressure isn’t on that, everyone’s just very happy and rich. The next quarter’s earnings are going to be where we start to see this shakeout. Can it keep growing the way it’s growing at the margins it needs to build everything, especially when its own suppliers are now major shareholders? Totally. And we saw one quarter where they experienced huge growth and then the next quarter wasn’t that much. So yeah, I mean they’re going to have a lot to reckon with. Let’s talk about the governance issues. Because of Nvidia, corporate governance is the hottest topic in American business. Like you said, OpenAI and Anthropic have some of the most complicated governance structures in history. If you think that Anthropic’s future is to sell the best intelligence — the most capable, the most cutting-edge frontier, close-to-AGI intelligence possible — you would probably not do a bunch of safety work. You would probably not kill your margins on a bunch of researchers who are telling you to stop or slow down or not release the best model. Anthropic is deeply committed to doing that. You and I have had conversations before about whether that can withstand the pressures of capitalism and growth. That was hard when they weren’t a public company, but now they are. Talk about Anthropic’s structure and how they’re trying to codify their commitment to safety. Yeah, that’s a really great question. I just published a piece about this . It’s so interesting to me that Anthropic, despite seeing all the roller-coaster drama that OpenAI went through around the Sam Altman ouster and all of the restructurings that that company has gone through, Anthropic has a similarly unusual structure. And in a way it’s helpful because they’re not beholden, as we said, to shareholder pressure besides if shareholders start selling off their stock or don’t buy more. But the two kinds of groups of people that have power over what happens at Anthropic are the founders and this group called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Anthropic likes to market this as being like, “Oh, don’t worry about that the founders are doing what’s best for humanity but with no checks. We’ve got this trust above us that can appoint or remove us anytime.” As we’ll see in the movie Artificial , Sam Altman famously says, “Oh, well, the board can fire me whenever.” He says that a million times . Now, Anthropic is implying the same thing: “Oh, we have this trust above us. They can remove or appoint the majority of board members,” even though it’s actually not all of them, but we’ll get to that in a minute. So this trust is a group of right now four people and none of them have a lot of AI experience. It’s [former Federal Reserve Chairman] Ben Bernanke, a foreign policy analyst named Richard Fontaine, an experimental physicist named Christopher Stubbs, and a former GiveWell executive named Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT. I spoke to a couple of former Anthropic employees that left not too long ago and one of them said that this trust is kind of handpicked to not rock the boat at Anthropic. The founders appointed them. They’re not going to be appointing someone that’s going to probably disagree with them a lot. Ironically, the trust doesn’t have the authority to step in on everyday decisions at Anthropic, unlike even the OpenAI nonprofit board that existed. They could say, “Oh look, don’t release this model. It’s too dangerous.” The trust doesn’t have any of those powers. All it can do is appoint or remove certain board members. Even then, they have to give 30 days’ notice to a small committee of the board, which includes Daniela Amodei, the chair of that little committee who is also a founder of Anthropic. To oversimplify things, out of these seven board seats, the trust gets to pick three, the founders get to pick three, and then the kind of tie-breaking seat, the seventh one, the trust technically appoints, but they have to basically get founder approval to do it. So it’s one of these things that’s so complex, but when you really look at the nitty-gritty of it, the founders have pretty unchecked control here. I think that’s something that’s getting lost in the narrative of, “Oh, this trust is above us. Don’t worry.” Okay, well, they don’t really have much power to check you. The founder control structure is the wildest thing I have ever read about in years of doing the show and thinking about business. Anthropic has seven founders. They have been issued a single share of stock that holds 50.1 percent of the voting power of the company. That is issued to a company called Founder LLC, and they’re the seven co-owners of Founder LLC. How on earth does that work? Do they just all get together and then decide how to vote the one share of stock? Yeah, it’s really interesting and that’s why I was kind of oversimplifying it a minute ago with who gets to choose this tie-breaking seat because it’s technically Founder LLC. It’s just a total mess. But when you really look at the simplified version, it’s that yes, through all of these weird structures and things they’ve done, they basically have pretty unchecked power and that’s the way they want it. When I was talking to a former employee who recently left, they said it’s not necessarily that the founders have a financial interest in making the most money. In their eyes, it’s more that they have an interest in unchecked control. I think that’s a really important point here. Some dissenters within the ranks of Anthropic think it’s not about them wanting to get rich, but rather it’s about them wanting that total control, which does track with a lot of their public statements. They say, “You can’t do safety from second place.” They’re all in on speeding up this race, but the problem is when you speed up the AI race, you’re speeding it up for everyone involved. The safety piece is the really interesting portion of this to me because it’s the thing you would spend money on, absent some huge litigation drama or liability concern, that no other company would spend money on. So let’s say it’s proven in court that model companies are liable for what people’s agents do. I think then all the model companies would build safety systems. They would have some big incentive to make sure their models are safe. That has not yet happened. We don’t know. There’s a big debate about safety and where the regulation will come from and what will create the incentives. In the meantime, you’ve got seven founders holding a single share of stock who right now appear to be aligned on investing in safety in various ways inside of Anthropic. What happens if they start to disagree? Yeah, that’s a great question. I think that the other interesting question here is what happens when you can explain away anything in the name of safety if you’re thinking it’s “for the greater good,” which as we know is a common villain trope in every movie. But it’s also one of Anthropic’s main things on its website . They’re like, “We want to do this for the greater good, for the global good.” If you’re saying, “Hey, we have to win this race at all costs because we’re the only good guys and anyone else who wins it is going to do worse than us,” are you really the good guy at that point? And can’t you just explain away any single decision, even dropping some safety measures, as saying, “Oh, it’s slowing us down too much. We’re going to lose. We’ve got to win at all costs”? So you drop this or drop that. And then you look in the mirror at the end of the race and you say, “Oh, actually, we’re the exact same as the other company we’re trying to be different from.” I think that’s increasingly happening. So I mean, right now they’ve said, “Look, we’re really committed to this.” You do have to remember that these people are almost religiously dedicated to this idea of safe AI. A lot of them think that AI systems are potentially conscious . I mean, this is by Anthropic founders’ own statements. So I think that it’s not like they’re just secretly only trying to make money and just talking about safety and they don’t mean it. I think it’s more something a little more dangerous in that they want complete control because they believe that they have the right plan for AI safety and they will do it better than anyone else. But as we know, absolute power corrupts absolutely. So a lot of Anthropic employees that I was talking to, former ones, were saying, “Yeah, it does not make sense that this industry is so unregulated. There’s no external regulation. Even if these seven people think they have the best idea for AI safety, okay, then prove it to someone else — that you shouldn’t be the only ones deciding this. Because you’re not elected.” So that’s the consensus among some. They have a morally binding handshake agreement to allow external auditors, Hayden. It’s going to be fine. Oh, yeah, with employee-level access. Also, it’s called “Super Intelligence” now. It’s going to be totally fine. They all went to the White House and they looked deeply into each other’s eyes and said it was going to be fine. Obviously Anthropic came up with this structure well before the events with Nvidia and Jensen Huang, but I can’t help but put them together in my head. They are happening at the same time. And Nvidia has a very traditional corporate governance structure. Jensen owned 3 percent of the company, but he had a board of directors. The board of directors determined that he had violated the company’s code of conduct in some way. He resigned. It’s very obvious that he was thoroughly encouraged to resign, but that’s just normal corporate governance. That’s what you learn about in school. A company has a board of directors. Their number one job is to hire and fire the CEO. That’s very different in Silicon Valley, right? Founder control of companies is a big story everywhere. Mark Zuckerberg famously has control over Meta, even though Meta shareholders repeatedly vote to remove him, which is one of the underemphasized stories in all of American business. Sergey Brin and Larry Page control Google. Is this more in the, “We need to insulate our founders from the demands of the market and boards of directors” in classic Silicon Valley style? Or is it, “We need to insulate our founders and Dario from the demands of the market so we can stay focused on AGI and safety”? Because it feels like a combination of both. It’s definitely a combination. I mean, they say it’s the latter. I think in a lot of ways it’s like the former. It’s totally a combination. I’d say it’s about 50/50. I mean, they want control so that they can focus on what they think is best and not lose control to someone that they don’t think knows best. But ironically, as we know, no one group of people should be in control of what is best here. So at least that’s what a lot of my sources say. So I think that, yeah, I mean, it’s just a combination. Elon Musk famously won’t run a company that he doesn’t have voting control over. So I think it’s just a new Valley thing and it’s pervading here for a couple of different reasons. There are seven of them. What seven different people do over the course of the next five to 10 years is as unpredictable as anything. What happens if one of them does something illegal or lies to the board or smuggles chips to China or anything? Is there some way to remove one of these founders from this LLC? Yeah. I mean, allegedly the trust has the power to remove. They haven’t said whether they have the power to remove all of the board or just some, but in some way when you’re looking at the fine print of the S-1, basically if the trust gives 30 days’ notice to essentially Daniela Amodei and her other two people on this subcommittee, then they can suggest removal of a board member. Again, they can waive that 30-day notice if they deem it correct, if Daniela does. But yeah, there’s a lot of fine print here. Essentially, yes, you can remove someone and there is stuff about that in the S-1 saying if they’ve done something illegal, if they’ve done something really bad, they can be removed, but it’s definitely not easy. It also depends on who it is, I think. It’s interesting. I keep coming back to this because it is so complicated, it’s so unusual, and it is right next to the Nvidia situation where he materially misrepresented his relationship to the shareholders by having his PR people issue statements saying it was all normal. He had to admit that it wasn’t all normal and he was in fact involved in extramarital affairs and the board fired him. I felt a little bad for that PR guy who had to put his name on all those statements that ended up being a lie. I feel nothing. As the audience may know, as Hayden is well aware, we make all the PR people put their names on everything just in case something like this happens. That’s just a little bit of Verge trivia. Anyhow, right, I mean, that’s just normal governance. Here you have a company where the only check might be the market itself, right? Yep. If they can’t sell tokens for more than what they make them for, they’re going to have to report that in the financials and the market might say this company is failing and pull all the money back. That is a very different kind of pressure. If the only meaningful way that Dario might lose his job is if the company goes bankrupt and then the swirl of things is he’s got to buy chips before OpenAI can buy the chips, he’s got to increase the number of verticals that Anthropic competes in within the enterprise, and he also idealistically has to train the next model and the next model with RSI to get to AGI, it feels like actually the pressure is to go as fast as possible. If I just added that up, I would say I would not slow down ever. Yeah. That’s why I say you can kind of explain away anything if you’re trying to be first, which they are. And they’ve been very public about that. Regarding the money thing, Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Law School, told me this week that the trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power and that you either trust that they’re going to balance the interest of society appropriately or you don’t. But either way, the real constraint on whatever impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money. That’s the thing, Anthropic needs money. In a livestream recently, Dario told the CEO of JPMorgan Chase that compute is the “deepest business dilemma” that the company faces. Essentially if you buy too much, you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers. Even more importantly, you can’t do the R&D. You can’t come up with new models. So they’re extremely compute-constrained, even maybe more so than OpenAI because OpenAI was made fun of for a long time for losing a ton of money, but they were investing a lot in compute. Anthropic did not do that as much, and now they’re having to pay the piper . So it’s an interesting turnaround here. Hopefully for them and their interests, I guess, if they can get the compute they need. But as we know, the supply is a lot lower than the demand. So it’s just going to be interesting to see what they will do to make money and therefore money to buy compute. It’s funny. A couple of weeks ago I told our colleague, Liz Lopatto, that the Anthropic IPO would be one of the biggest stories of the year. She was laughing at me today, because she says it’s not even the biggest story of the week because of Jensen Huang and Nvidia. My argument — take it or leave it, and you can judge whether I’m correct — is that they are the same story. That if Nvidia’s financing architecture fails or wobbles because Jensen isn’t there to bully everyone into believing in it, then maybe you do have a glut of chips sitting in data centers without the appropriate permitting or power to light them up and the market for chips will change dramatically. Maybe a company like CoreWeave does get way more wobbly or some of the already wobbly neoclouds start to get wobbly and the price of compute falls and lets Anthropic compete differently. Maybe a bunch of chips that were allocated to China on the gray market come flooding back to the United States. That apparently will happen. Right? So there’s a lot of ways the Nvidia story affects Anthropic’s financials. Has the company said anything about that yet? Is the market reacting to that in any way? Not yet. They’ve just talked about how important compute is and that it’s going to be a really big issue for them. And Anthropic’s IPO, it has a lot of ties to Nvidia and there’s a lot of complexities here because Nvidia had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement on top of a $10 billion funding promise it made last year. So they are in bed together, and that’s going to be interesting to see, too. The new CEO of Nvidia has made a lot of claims about diverting chips that were potentially going to China and bringing them back so they’re not doing that anymore. Now we’re going to see if there’s more supply or not. Also, Jensen personally made some of these deals, especially with large financial institutions to fund the AI infrastructure buildout last August. So he’s wheeling and dealing a lot. And so it’s going to remain to be seen whether the new chief executive has that kind of power to wheel and deal and pressure people into doing stuff like this or not. This is my last question. Obviously everyone’s just celebrating today. We are probably throwing the most cold water on this by noting that the structure of Anthropic is very odd. What should people be looking for? What are the signs that you’re looking for now that Anthropic is a stock that’s trading? What’s the relationship in your mind between the value of Anthropic stock on any given day and the broader AI story? I think that stock is a little bit like benchmarks in the AI industry in that sometimes it doesn’t mean what you think it means and also it never means everything. So you always take it with a grain of salt. It’s all vibes based. It’s all hype. So people get scared, they sell, and people hear one good thing or a rumor and they buy. So I think it’s important to look at it and see what’s driving that fear or hype that day or that week. But it’s also really important to see what the company says in these reports and earnings calls. That’s what I think is the most interesting. Not really the numbers all the time, but instead, what they try to sneak into these reports by saying, “Oh, we sidelined this team,” or, “We discontinued this safety initiative all in the name of being first.” That’s the type of thing that I think we’re going to see a lot of and that’s what I want to watch for. Because the company that made its bed on safe AI is increasingly looking the same as OpenAI and is going to have a lot of swept-under-the-rug type of updates like that, if my sources are right. You heard it here first. Former CNBC reporter Hayden Field says, look past the day-to-day swings into the fundamentals of the company. That’s good. Also, the stock market is only vibes. That’s the other thing I heard you say. Yep. I mean, it’s controversial, but after being a financial reporter, yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of vibes there. It’s a lot of vibes. Oh, I agree. I think sometimes the only thing they ask me to go on CNBC to say is this is just vibes, and then they usher me off the air very quickly. Hayden, this is great. We’re obviously going to be talking about this story many times with you in the year to come. Hopefully we can do another straightforward business story and not just a soap opera one. I’ll be here for both. We’ve got to do them both. Amazing. Thank you so much, Hayden. Thanks. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!

articles.fullContent: Hebbia 在 GPT‑6 Astra 的测试中看到了金融研究方面的收益。 在 Hebbia 的测试中，领先于表现最佳的替代方案的百分点数。 在 Hebbia 的测试中，与问题相关的引用摘录的百分比。 Hebbia 测试中满足适用呈现要求的百分比。 在演示文稿要求方面，领先于所测试的最佳替代方案的百分点数。 在向客户推荐收购之前，银行家需要弄清财务报表、客户合同和管理层演示文稿。 Hebbia 的 Matrix 有助于整合这些研究，将答案与背后的文件联系起来。 Hebbia 测试了 OpenAI 的 GPT‑6 Astra，以改进这项工作的两个方面：找到问题所需的来源，并根据银行家的简要说明制作演示文稿。 具体运作方式可能是这样的：一位银行家正在帮助客户评估对一家工业软件公司的战略收购，需要审核大约 2000 个文件。 是什么让其收入具有可持续性？ 它与同行相比如何？ 在Hebbia的假设示例中，银行家可以将数据室加载到Matrix中，并在引用的单元格中查看客户集中度、合同条款和流失率。 Matrix可以引入同行备案和行业新闻，帮助制定交易论证，然后将该研究转化为公司的模板中的尽职调查摘要和估值演示文稿。 在该工作流程中，GPT‑6 Astra 会选择文件或 Matrix 单元格来支持答案，然后将分析转换为遵循用户结构和指南的原生 PowerPoint 幻灯片。 “可追溯性对我们的用户来说非常重要，因为他们要根据 AI 实际给出的结果来做出价值数百万美元的决策，”Kavita 表示。 “引用有助于实现可追溯性，并让用户确信人工智能找到了正确的答案。” 在 Hebbia 的测试中，GPT‑6 Astra 将更广泛的来源覆盖范围与高度相关的引用相结合。它获得了 13 分。 在引用所需类型的来源方面，比测试的最佳替代方案高出6个百分点，而其引用的摘录中有99.5%与问题相关。 Hebbia 于 2026 年 8 月至 9 月测试了一个预发布版本，对每个模型使用了相同的金融研究案例和评分标准。 领域专家根据源文档撰写或审核了标准。

articles.fullContent: 我们如何应对蒸馏的安全风险，以及我们在加强整个行业的安全保障方面所吸取的经验教训。 随着前沿人工智能模型的能力不断增强，保障措施在如何负责任地使用这些模型方面发挥着越来越重要的作用。 对抗性蒸馏为不法分子在没有适当保障措施的情况下复制这些能力开辟了一条途径。 行为者可能会在未经授权的情况下使用前沿模型的输出，来训练另一个具有类似功能的模型，然后将其部署，而没有提供同等水平的保护。 例如，攻击者可能会提炼出一个模型的网络能力，并使用由此产生的模型来帮助实施网络攻击，而原始模型本会拒绝协助此类攻击，或者其安全防护措施本会阻止此类攻击。 我们将分享OpenAI如何检测和阻止对抗性蒸馏，我们如何加强对模型受保护推理的保护，以及我们学到了哪些可以帮助加强整个行业的防御措施的经验。 我们处理对抗性蒸馏的方法将对抗性测试、模型训练、分类器和API级保护与对有组织地提取模型能力的企图的调查相结合。 这些更新后的保障措施与我们在生物学和网络安全领域所采用的措施更加一致。 我们特别重视防止攻击者提取我们模型的受保护推理：即模型在努力得出答案的过程中在内部生成的中间步骤，称为其“思维链”。 这些痕迹可能包含最终答案中未提及的信息，因此它们对于另一个模型来说是特别有价值的训练数据。 我们在 GPT‑6 中加强了针对受保护推理提取的防御。2 Astra 和 GPT‑6。2 Sol。在一次使用强大自动化红队的内部自适应评估中，我们测试了攻击者是否能够恢复模型在回答先前提示时生成的受保护推理。 平均攻击成功率从针对具有原始安全防护措施的 GPT‑6 Astra 的 54. 0% 下降到针对具有更新版安全防护措施的 GPT‑6. 2 Astra（采用更新后的安全措施）的攻击成功率降至 0.2%。 蒸馏是一种常见的机器学习技术，其中一个模型从另一个模型产生的数据中学习。 例如，一个模型可以从另一个模型的答案、其推理或其对哪些答案更好以及为什么更好的判断中学习。 除了知识产权问题外，未经授权的蒸馏还会带来严重的安全风险。 通过对抗性蒸馏，第二个模型可以学习先进的前沿能力，而无需继承规范原始模型如何使用这些能力的保障措施。 在网络安全和生物学等双用途领域，这种担忧尤为明显。 一个帮助防御者发现软件漏洞的模型也可能帮助攻击者利用这些漏洞；一个协助生物学研究的模型也可能帮助某人开发有害病原体。 如果将此类能力转移到具有较弱保障措施的模型，该模型可能会提供原始模型会拒绝或原始保障措施会阻止的帮助。 我们的模型可帮助用户完成编码和防御性网络安全任务。 在许多此类良性输出上进行训练的第二个模型可能会学到同样适用于进攻性网络安全任务的技能。

articles.rawFullText: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest. Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark. The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do. Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions: What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution. Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds. Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step. Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows. Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle. The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption. Explore how UL Solutions builds trust in AI . This content was produced by UL Solutions. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff.

articles.fullContent: 多年来，企业一直将人工智能视为一系列独立的实验。 如今，随着人工智能代理开始进入支撑业务运营的工作流程，这种模式开始显得力不从心。 从孤立的试点转向 AI 代理和自主工作流程的组织正面临着一个更深层次的挑战：重新思考数据、业务流程、治理和人员如何相互配合，将 AI 从一系列工具转变为企业运营模式的一部分。 对于SAP业务人工智能平台生态系统高级副总裁兼全球负责人Thorsten Leiduck来说，这种转变始于将人工智能视为一个企业平台，而不是一系列互不关联的项目。 “人工智能完全依赖于数据基础，”他表示，并认为企业需要一个互联且语义丰富的层来反映其业务，然后才能在各个流程中可靠地部署人工智能。 随着人工智能进入任务关键型工作流程，其利害关系也会发生变化。 他说，对于一些日常应用来说，“80%可能就足够好了”，但在供应链或财务结算等领域，这样的准确率“是一个非常糟糕的结果”。这一基础还决定了哪些人工智能应用值得追求。 Infosys SAP BAIP和SAP AI战略北美区副总裁Satinder Pal Singh将AI代理称为“数字同事”，并建议从三个角度评估潜在用例：影响、可行性和可扩展性。 公司应确定代理可以在哪些方面推动有意义的业务指标，确定其数据和人才是否能够支持该用例，然后确定成功的应用是否可以复制。 “无法扩展的试点项目只是一项实验，”他说。 扩展还会使治理问题更加突出。 明确的政策、访问控制、监控和监督是必要的，以确保代理始终值得信赖并符合业务要求。 “缺乏治理并不会加快人工智能的采用，”Singh 表示。 “它会造成风险积压”，最终可能迫使企业进行更具破坏性的停用和审计。 随着人工智能代理作为数字同事承担更多责任，这些考虑因素将变得更加重要。 两位高管都展望着一个未来，即代理系统协调跨应用程序的工作，而针对具体客户的知识图谱和受管控的数据将成为关键的企业资产。 在Singh看来，长期的机会在于将人工智能从生产力工具转变为“决策合作伙伴”，帮助领导者了解当前情况、预测未来发展并确定应对方式。 本期《商业实验室》由Infosys合作制作。

articles.rawFullText: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.” That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says. Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit. Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond. This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Infosys. Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace. This episode is produced in partnership with Infosys. Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. But, at a time when applications are being scaled up from that initial phase of experimentation, we’re still seeing senior leaders grapple with questions around AI’s value, risk, and the complexity it adds. It’s becoming clear that, unlike past ways of automation, AI requires a real mindset shift. Put simply, the technology can’t simply be added into an enterprise’s existing toolkit. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used. Two words for you: conscious configuration. My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy. Welcome, Thorsten and Satinder. Thorsten Leiduck: Yeah, thank you for having us. Really a pleasure to be here with our valued partner, Infosys. Looking forward to the conversation. Satinder Pal Singh: Hi, Megan. Thanks for inviting for the conversation today. Looking forward to the discussion. Megan: Me too. Thank you both so much for being here. Thorsten, if I could start with you. We know that many senior leaders understand the transformative potential in AI, but they continue to struggle with aspects of its implementation. Many projects remain stuck at a pilot phase, for example. When you speak to clients, what are the biggest obstacles they face when it comes to integrating AI into their tech stack? Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation. This creates a lot of duplication, inconsistent performance, and no clear path to scale. At the same time, leaders are highly concerned about security, observability, reliability of agents, and some ethical implications when those get deployed. This is also shown in some studies. For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. And in an Anthropic survey, data said that 42% are really struggling with getting access to the data and the quality to really, basically, scale the entire AI capabilities across the organization. The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. And to make this real, we in SAP launched the SAP autonomous enterprise framework, so organizations can move from pilots to scaled outcomes. Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we’re seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What’s the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well? Satinder: Absolutely, Megan. And, if anything, the picture sharpens when you look at, specifically, at agentic AI. Infosys and HFS research surveyed over 500 global 2,000 enterprises and found only 14% have successfully scaled AI. Eighty-six percent remain in early exploration, proof of concept, or fragmented pilot phases. For a technology at the top of every boardroom agenda for two years, that’s a striking failure rate. And at the core of that 86% is what I would describe as AI as a department trap. What happens is that an organization creates an AI team or a center of excellence and walls it off from business. That team builds technically excellent pilots the business doesn’t recognize itself in, and you end up with AI solutions searching for problems, rather than the other way around. Mindset shift is clear. Move from treating AI as a technology initiative to treating it as an operating model transformation. AI stops being something IT does for business and starts being something the whole organization does together. Every function, every workflow, embedded from the start. And what makes this a now problem? Early movers are building an advantage. You cannot close by buying the same platform later. Eighteen months of agent behavior data, calibrated knowledge graph, workforce that has genuinely internalized AI, that is a structural advantage that compounds. Infosys Knowledge Institute AI Maturity Index shows that only 8% of the companies qualify as AI native today, yet they achieve four times the revenue contribution from the AI versus laggards. If you’re not building AI today, you’re not standing still, you’re falling behind at an accelerating rate. Megan: Right. There’s a real polarization there, isn’t there, between the front-runners and the laggards, as you say. As we shift from pilot to scaled-up applications, perhaps the first step is evaluating when AI is the right tool. AI has quickly become the default solution within many enterprises. Is there a tendency to use it as a bit of a blunt instrument, nowadays, Thorsten? At the outset, how can senior leaders better evaluate what use cases are worthy of their time and investment, in order to strip out some of that later complexity? Thorsten: Yeah, I think, Megan, what everybody needs to be aware is adopting and rolling out AI across an organization is as much a change management journey as it’s a technology rollout. Now, when you have this in mind, it makes absolutely sense to put AI in front as many teams as possible, because you want to build formality, and spark ideas, and also people should see the benefit of AI in an organization. When you think about travel assistance, meeting summaries via Copilot, or AI-enabled workflows, increase the productivity, everybody feels this in their real job, in their real daily business. And, obviously, this creates creativity and also provides the organization from a bottom-up perspective with some innovation scale. Now, however, as majority grows, the conversation, and this is also what we discuss with many of the leaders, and our clients, shifts more to economics and governance. Things like token costs, model performance, security, and accountability become much more relevant. And when you then take the approach and think about AI agents as digital workers that execute specific tasks within a business process, then this means, from an AI perspective, not every task justifies nation. In some cases, human effort remains more economical or effective. The smart approach, and that’s what we really recommend to our clients, is to start with a defined, maybe small set of high-value use cases with defined success metrics upfront. So, for example, such as cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, or cost of per transaction, or top line improvement, and then scale what works. Those use cases can be tied to a line of business domains or industry scenarios. And then, what we are doing from an SAP perspective, together with Infosys, we really help customers to be successful. We provide, as part of our autonomous suite, the according domain assistance, which really run business processes end-to-end and which deliver find ROIs for single end-to-end business process steps. And then, last but not least, in many scenarios, I think, which has been very common pattern in particular around large industry AI use cases, is a joint approach, and we do this with partners like Infosys, but also customers around forward deployed engineering, so that you really define very closely the AI-specific use case with the defined outcomes together with the customer, and deliver this as the initial projects. And then, ideally, scale this to other customers and take it back like a best practice, which can be rolled out to other organizations, as well. Megan: Right. It’s been really clear, isn’t it, on what you’re looking to achieve and what’s worth your time, as I say. And what would your advice, Satinder, be here, on refining an AI strategy to ensure organizations can focus on those areas, where AI can deliver the highest returns? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten’s framing of AI agents as digital coworkers forces a precision that agentic AI strategy language often lacks. When you ask which digital coworkers do we need and where do they deliver the most value, the answer starts to become clearer right from the first step. At Infosys, through our Topaz AI-first framework, we push clients through the three lenses simultaneously. The first one is impact. Where does deploying an agent move the numbers that matter? Revenue, cost, working capital risk. We have built a library of over 300 enterprise use cases across industries, so we never begin from a blank page. The second is feasibility. Given your data foundation platform and talent today, which high-impact use cases can you actually execute? Feasibility determines your sequence. The high-impact use case on a broken data foundation is not viable. When the foundation is right, the results are dramatic. One Infosys engagement cut complex SAP-specification documents from 86 person hours to 6, a 92% reduction. Third is scalability. Once you have proven a use case with clear ROI metrics, cycle time reduction, accuracy gains, cost per transaction, what’s the architecture that lets you replicate it? A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment. My practical advice: treat your AI portfolio like an investment portfolio, quick wins that fund the program, medium-term bets, one or two bold, long-term positions that balance keep stakeholders engaged at every stage and not just in year three. Megan: That’s such a useful framework for people to use there. And given the urgency here, Thorsten, how can organizations approach and manage AI in a more structured, efficient way? To start with, what are the fundamentals that some organizations perhaps miss at the moment? I know Infosys and SAP talk about platform and data, then AI, for example. Thorsten: Yeah, Megan, I think the fundamental, which many organizations are overlooking, is data and the data is a foundation for AI. Because, at the end, without the data structures and the ability to access the right information at the right time and basically bringing different kind of structured, unstructured data sources together, in a meaningful governed and semantic way, there will be no successful AI. AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation. And I think this is often overlooked, and that’s why I said when you start POCs in different organization, or different parts of the organization with different technologies, it’s very hard to establish an end-to-end consistent model on the data side, as well as on the AI side. One of the key goals companies need to achieve is, and that’s why we really talk about you need to start with data first and the platform first, is to establish and semantically-rich connected data layer that really reflects your business, so that the agents are really grounded in the company’s reality and not just in generic patterns. And then, I think, the second element that’s important is accuracy. In the enterprise context, it really matters. For example, what might pass in a consumer setting, where you have 80% accuracy, and even in a workforce environment where you build PowerPoints or you do email drafts, which you then, with a human in the loop, optimize, 80% might be good enough. But, when you really think about mission-critical or business-critical processes in the supply chain, or closing the books, 80% is a very terrible result. The stakes are much too high and you need to have much more accuracy. And that’s why it’s important that you have business process logic and industry context embedded into the data and the models which build the foundation, if you will, the backbone for every AI and, obviously, for the data in the ERP and the line of business system. And then, last but not least, the other critical element, and you see this obviously in the news with all the agents going rogue, are governance, compliance, and security. Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable. Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI’s capability a little bit easier? Satinder: Megan, I think at the onset, I want to acknowledge that, at Infosys, we are uniquely positioned for our relationship with SAP, because we are a customer to SAP, as well as one of their key global suppliers. And the way SAP and Infosys work together is designed around the architecture Thorsten described, that defines a coherent partnership. SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. We co-develop use cases within SAP’s industry AI engagement with clear customer-specific FTE metrics. That shared accountability for results is different from a typical implementation engagement. In practice, one global S/4HANA transformation program used AI-assisted delivery tooling to complete over 480 RICEF objects in five months, a pace conventional delivery would not sustain. In another account, an AI-powered platform auto-classifies over 120,000 SAP incidents monthly, with zero analyst charge. The combined effect time to value drops from 12 to 18 months, down to four to six months. What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What’s hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations . That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel. Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP’s Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms? Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars. The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP’s own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed. Complimenting what Satinder said, it’s really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don’t cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together. Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. For the customer, this is very important. So, we allow, basically, promote to customers if you have made investments in any of those platforms, reserve those investments and just leverage BDC to connect without moving data around your, for example, Databricks, Snowflake environment to BDC. With this approach, we establish and harmonize semantic data layer, which can then be used for any AI scenario across the entire enterprise, combining different data sources without any disruption. The other key element that’s part of this is the generative AI hub. We have aggregated more than 50 models, language models, including some of our own models into it, in single cockpit, so that customers can access and choose any of those 50 models as part of the generative-AI hub, which is part of the platform. And then, as a key differentiator, we really moved a lot of business semantic and context into the knowledge graph, which then helps to navigate the agents and acts like a nerve, or navigation system, in the company to really provide business-relevant, customer-specific information for the decision making and the execution to any agentic execution framework. And then, we talked about governance, last but not least. This is the third pillar, which is very critical and this is built-in. So, we have, as the third pillar, the SAP agent hub, which is kind of a command center for enterprise-wide AI and agent governments. You can govern SAP agents, you can also govern non-SAP agents, as long as they’re integrating to SAP via A2A. So, the team can really manage, on the customer side, an end-to-end life cycle of agents and features from hire to retire. Megan: Fantastic. That’s a really comprehensive overview. Thank you ever so much. And, Satinder, can you share any examples, perhaps, of how organizations have used SAP Business AI Platform in practice, to improve the ways they’ve used AI? Perhaps, what was the challenge they faced, what did the process look like, and what benefits did they unlock? Satinder: Sure, Megan. I think Thorsten just explained how powerful a platform Business AI Platform is. And this is decades in working. We also have been using that, and I’ll share two examples from live Infosys engagements, both showing what BIP’s three pillar look like in production. The first is global diversified manufacturer with a large SAP estate. The challenge was month-end close, 80-plus SAP transaction codes, period closed teams working nights and weekends, L1 support absorbing over 300 incidents per month, from close cycle alone. On Business AI Platform, we deployed Topaz Fabric, Infosys’ agentic orchestration platform, with a master agent coordinating five specialist child agents, WBS accrual, revenue recognition, intercompany settlement, master data reconciliation, and SOX audit trail generation. Agents run autonomously, escalating to humans only for genuine exceptions. The result, entire L1.5 support tier eliminated, over 300 monthly incidents handled with zero human touch. The close team redeployed from reactive firefighting to forward-looking financial analysis. Annual savings pipeline exceed $1 million. The second is North American Utility in a S/4HANA transformation. Their challenge was development velocity, complex SAP functional specification documents routinely requiring 80 or more personnel each, a bottleneck throttling the entire program. Using AI native development environment on Business AI Platform with a Claude-powered retrieval system, we reduced those specifications from 86 hours to six, a 92% reduction, validated across 51 SAP task types at 95% accuracy. The architecture is now being replicated across accounts. In both cases, the pattern matches what Thorsten described, governed data foundation, SAP business process context, full agent observability through SAP Agent Hub. That’s the autonomous enterprise running as daily operations, not as a concept. Megan: And those are some really compelling concrete results I think would be really helpful for people to hear. Also, of course, responsible AI, or clear governance frameworks, are a critical component of AI integration, too. And we know that tools like LLMs are rarely developed with compliance built-in. I wonder what’s your advice there, Thorsten, on how to ensure that property governance is embedded into an ERP? Thorsten: Yeah, I mean, Megan, you’re absolutely right. Governance compliance and security are really mission-critical to delivering relevant, reliable, and trustworthy AI at enterprise scale. I mean, it’s important to understand how in public LLM service really works. Many of those services are trained on internet scale data, which means they’re public models. Depending on the provider’s policies and setting, they may retain easier inputs for model improvement, which means if a company provides data back to the model, this company data is in the public domain. For example, pipeline information or forecast information, which is becoming very, very critical, because this exposes your organization, really, at significant risk. So, while then LLMs X are really great, imposes in large volumes of text and other unstructured data, they are less effective with structured tables like in EOP systems, or in business applications, in general, and then they’re lacking, usually, the nuance of business process and logic and context. That’s why a robust governance framework is essential. We talked about the generative AI, how we aggregate those models in a single cockpit. And then, the other element, which we previously touched based on and Satinder mentioned, is always a part of the custom examples is SAP agent hub or, in general, when we talk about the capabilities just in AI lifecycle governance, which really includes agent registry, LMN registries, MCP registry, so a single source of tool for every AI artifact that you can manage identity and access control, so that agents are really variable and that you can really provide the right permissions, in terms of which agents allowed to use access which data, and then agent observability, agent minus, and then also map the agent skills to the organization is very critical. As all of part of this, as I mentioned before, we provide those capabilities really fully embedded into the Business AI Platform to really provide this governance framework out of the box and fully embedded into everything what you do at SAP. Megan: Which is so important, because when organizations are experimenting with, or scaling up multiple AI programs and tools, in some cases, it adds real complexity. I wonder, Satinder, would you add anything on how organizations can have that robust layer of governance built in, even with a pretty complex tech stack? Satinder: We, at Infosys, have our Infosys Knowledge Institute, they run this annual magazine generative AI radar, and it found that 48% of companies had deployed generative AI without a formal governance policy. Nearly half of the enterprises were running AI with no documented framework or oversight, accountability, or compliance. That’s the gap that Thorsten is describing, and it has to be closed proactively before an incident forces a reactive stop or audit far more disruptive than building a governance upfront. What Thorsten has just described in SAP Agent Hub is exactly the platform layer that makes enterprise-wide governance possible and is worth making the overall architecture explicit, because without it, governance is theoretical. The framework I use with clients has three layers that have to work together. The first one is policy, a clear organization-wide AI use policy, what agents can and cannot do autonomously, how data can be used for AI training, disclosure obligations, and accountability for outcomes. This needs legal, compliance, technology teams together with a board level sponsorship. Without that foundation, every deployment becomes an ad hoc governance debate. Second layer is platform. This is where SAP Business AI Platform and, specifically, SAP Agent Hub becomes enterprise control tower. The capabilities Thorsten described, agent LLM, MCP registry as a single source of truth, verifiable agent identities with scoped access trails, agent observability, agent mining for drift detection, these aren’t just governance features. They give leaders real-time visibility across a complex multi-agent landscape. You can see what’s running, what it’s consuming, and whether it’s performing as expected. That’s what turns a complex tech stack from a governance liability to a governance asset. And the last layer is process, the recurring governance rituals, quarterly AI risk reviews, bias audit cycles, model performance reviews against the business KPIs, these structured conversations that keep humans accountable for the agent behavior over time. What organizations consistently discover is that this three-layer structure actually accelerates the deployment. Every new use case has a clear path through approval and a governance architecture to plug into. The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption. It creates a risk backlog that eventually forces a stop and audit movement far more disruptive than building the governance muscle. Megan: That’s such an interesting point. Thank you so much for that. And we’ve covered a lot of ground, so to close with a future forward look, we’ve spoken today about the proliferation of AI tools that are now on the market, many designed to transform enterprise-level operations. I wonder, what do you see on the horizon, Thorsten, that you think could be a real game-changer? On the technology front, I think there’s still so much movement on the LLM landscape, new architectures, training methods. I think we’ll bring down, significantly, the total cost of ownership, while also control and the viability will be improved. I think there’s an awareness which the recent examples in the market show, and then I think the innovation will be playable.
